power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.130", "p = 0.795"), Sentence = c("BMI category distributions did not differ between groups (p = 0.130; Supplementary Table 1).", "Among APOE ε4 non-carriers, males had higher dementia risk than females (male vs female OR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.07-1.55, p = 0.007), whereas no significant sex difference was observed among APOE ε4 carriers (male vs female OR = 0.98, 95% CI 0.83-1.15, p = 0.795)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Sex and APOE ε4 influence dementia risk, but whether its molecular predictors differ across sex and APOE ε4 strata remains unclear.
We investigated plasma proteomic and metabolomic signatures predicting future dementia in 43,759 UK Biobank participants across four sex-by-APOE ε4 groups.
The association between APOE ε4 carrier status and dementia differed by sex (interaction p = 0.027).
Machine-learning models achieved higher discrimination in APOE ε4 carriers (AUC 0.85-0.90) than non-carriers (AUC 0.74-0.76), with the highest performance in female carriers.
Most top molecular predictors were subgroup-specific, including C7, CDON and EDIL3 in female carriers and KLK4, MMP12 and TGFBI in male carriers.
When UK Biobank models were applied to the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium, 12/17 available top predictors in female carriers and 10/16 in male carriers remained highly ranked.
These findings identify distinct molecular signatures of dementia risk across sex and APOE ε4 strata, supporting stratified biomarker discovery.
Dementia is a leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide, affecting over 50 million people, with prevalence projected to exceed 150 million by 2050 (1).

text.text: Beyond age, sex and APOE ε4 genotype are two of the strongest risk factors for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD) (2).

text.text: APOE ε4 carriers have increased dementia risk, with homozygotes exhibiting up to 15-fold higher AD risk than APOE ε3 homozygotes (3).

text.text: An APOE-stratified genome-wide association study further identified genetic associations that differ according to APOE carrier status, suggesting distinct genetic mechanisms contributing to AD (4).

text.text: Females are disproportionately affected by dementia (2, 5), with some studies reporting greater APOE ε4-associated risk in females than males (6).

text.text: Nevertheless, dementia risk prediction studies have largely focused on population-level models, with less attention to the molecular heterogeneity underlying risk across sex and APOE ε4 subgroups.

Identifying subgroup-specific molecular signatures before clinical dementia onset may clarify heterogeneity in neurodegeneration, provide insights into the biological basis of variation in dementia risk, and inform future precision prevention strategies (14).

text.text: High-throughput plasma proteomics and metabolomics enable minimally invasive investigation of molecular changes associated with neurodegeneration.
Machine learning can further model complex relationships within high-dimensional biological data and is increasingly applied to dementia research (15) (16) (17) (18).

text.text: However, whether the molecular features driving dementia prediction differ across sex and APOE ε4 strata remains insufficiently characterised.
Furthermore, external validation, cross-platform transportability, and biological interpretation of machine learningderived molecular signatures remain limited.
Using UK Biobank (UKB) (20) as a prospective discovery cohort, we integrated plasma proteomics and metabolomics within sex and APOE ε4 strata to identify molecular signatures of future dementia risk.

We evaluated the cross-cohort and cross-platform transportability of the identified proteomic signatures in the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) (21), a clinically enriched cohort using a distinct proteomic platform.

This allowed us to examine the contributions of molecular predictors without chronological age entering the models directly, although age-related biological variation may still be reflected in the selected proteins.

text.text: APOE ε4 carriers shared five proteins among their top-ranked features (BCAN, APOE, CA14, CEND1 and CDCP1), whereas non-carriers shared only LTBP2 and ELN.
Additional overlaps included VGF in both male strata and SYT1 across female carriers, female non-carriers and male carriers.
Across all four groups, GFAP, NEFL and GDF15 were the only proteins consistently represented among the top predictors.

Proteins dominated the top-ranked predictors, with two metabolomic measures (XXL_VLDL_C_pct and XXL_VLDL_TG_pct, representing the cholesterol and triglyceride content of extremely large VLDL particles) appearing among the top predictors only in male APOE ε4 non-carriers.
These findings suggest that the molecular features contributing to dementia prediction differ substantially across sex and APOE ε4 strata.

text.text: Among APOE ε4 carriers, proteins contributing more strongly to prediction in females were enriched for GPCR ligand binding and downstream signalling, metabolism, cytokine signalling, gene transcription and extracellular matrix organisation.

In contrast, proteins contributing more strongly to prediction in males were enriched for innate immune system processes, MAPK signalling cascades, receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, developmental biology, regulation of insulin-like growth factor transport and protein metabolism (Figure 4A).

text.text: A different pattern was observed among APOE ε4 non-carriers.
Female-associated predictors were enriched for pathways related to signal transduction, immune system processes and protein metabolism.
In contrast, male-associated predictors were enriched for extracellular matrix organisation and broader metabolic pathways (Figure 4B).

text.text: Although these findings did not survive correction for multiple testing and should therefore be considered exploratory, they suggest potentially distinct biological processes underlying the sex and APOE ε4-specific molecular signatures.

text.text: Higher SYT1 and GDF15 levels were also consistently associated with increased odds of all dementia-related outcomes.
In contrast, lower BCAN and CDON levels were associated with increased odds of AD and all-cause dementia.
These inverse associations were consistent with SHAP patterns in UKB and GNPC, where lower levels contributed towards higher dementia risk predictions.
Patterns of statistical significance varied across dementia outcomes.

BCAN, CDON, and LRIG3 showed significant associations with AD and all-cause dementia, but not vascular dementia, whereas CXCL9 and EDIL3 showed significant associations with all-cause dementia and vascular dementia.
C7 and DCN reached statistical significance only for all-cause dementia.

Of the 13 proteins tested, 9 (C1QL2, GDF15, GFAP, KHK, KLK4, MMP12, NEFL, SYT1 and TGFBI) were significantly associated with at least one dementia-related outcome after FDR correction (Figure 6B; Supplementary Table 40).

GFAP and NEFL were significantly associated with all three dementia outcomes in both female and male non-carriers.

text.text: In this study, we applied a stratified machine learning framework integrating plasma proteomics and metabolomics to characterise sex-APOE ε4-specific molecular signatures predictive of future dementia risk.

To our knowledge, this is among the first studies combining sex-stratified APOE ε4 analyses with multimodal omics, interpretable machine learning, and external cross-platform validation to investigate molecular heterogeneity underlying dementia risk.
Figure 7 integrates the principal molecular risk patterns identified across analytical approaches.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">7</ref> integrates the principal molecular risk patterns identified across analytical approaches.

text.text: Three principal findings emerged.
First, molecular signatures differed substantially across sex-APOE ε4 strata, revealing both shared and subgroup-specific molecular predictors.
Second, APOE ε4 carriers demonstrated stronger molecular predictive signals than non-carriers, with female carriers showing the highest model discrimination.

Third, several proteomic predictors and SHAP-derived feature importance rankings were preserved in GNPC despite differences in cohort composition, disease stage, outcome definition and proteomic platform.
These findings support partial cross-cohort transportability of molecular predictor importance.
One notable observation was the stronger predictive performance among APOE ε4 carriers compared with non-carriers, accompanied by a larger number of stable Boruta-selected features.

This may reflect more consistent molecular associations with dementia risk among carriers, potentially driven by a greater contribution of Alzheimer's disease pathology to dementia outcomes in this group.

This interpretation is biologically plausible given the involvement of APOE ε4 in amyloid accumulation (22, 23), neuroinflammation (24,25), lipid dysregulation (26), synaptic dysfunction (27), and blood-brain barrier impairment (28).
text.formatted: This interpretation is biologically plausible given the involvement of APOE ε4 in amyloid accumulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">23)</ref>, neuroinflammation (24,25), lipid dysregulation (26), synaptic dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(27)</ref>, and blood-brain barrier impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(28)</ref>.

text.text: However, differences in dementia case numbers, case composition and statistical power may also contribute to the observed differences in model performance and feature selection.
Distinct molecular signatures emerged among female and male APOE ε4 carriers, reflecting differences in immune signalling, tissue remodelling, neuronal communication and metabolic processes.

These patterns were supported by the integration of machine learning feature importance, exploratory pathway enrichment, cross-cohort preservation of selected predictors and conventional association analyses.
Several female APOE ε4 carrier-specific predictors demonstrated substantial preservation across cohorts, including C7, EDIL3, CDON, LRIG3, CXCL9 and DCN.

C7, a component of the complement system, implicates inflammatory processes relevant to AD pathology (29, 30), while EDIL3 (31, 32) and DCN (33) point towards vascular regulation and extracellular matrix organisation.
text.formatted: C7, a component of the complement system, implicates inflammatory processes relevant to AD pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">30)</ref>, while EDIL3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">32)</ref> and DCN (33) point towards vascular regulation and extracellular matrix organisation.

text.text: CXCL9 (34), a chemokine involved in immune cell recruitment and inflammatory signalling, further supports the immune-related component of this signature.
text.formatted: CXCL9 <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(34)</ref>, a chemokine involved in immune cell recruitment and inflammatory signalling, further supports the immune-related component of this signature.

text.text: CDON (35) and LRIG3 (36), which participate in developmental and growth factor signalling, further point towards neurodevelopmental processes and cell-to-cell communication.
text.formatted: CDON <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(35)</ref> and LRIG3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(36)</ref>, which participate in developmental and growth factor signalling, further point towards neurodevelopmental processes and cell-to-cell communication.

text.text: Together, these findings highlight a female APOE ε4 carrier signature spanning immune and inflammatory signalling, tissue homeostasis and neurodevelopmental processes, extending beyond established markers of neurodegeneration.
In contrast, male APOE ε4 carriers showed enrichment for innate immune processes, MAPK signalling, receptor tyrosine kinase pathways, developmental biology, and growth factor signalling.
Several male-specific predictors, including MMP12, TGFBI, SCARF2, KLK4, C1QL2 and KHK, showed preservation across cohorts.

KLK4, which ranked among the strongest predictors in UKB and was the highest-ranked predictor in GNPC, has previously been implicated in plasma proteomic signatures of Alzheimer's disease, dementia and cognitive decline (37).
text.formatted: KLK4, which ranked among the strongest predictors in UKB and was the highest-ranked predictor in GNPC, has previously been implicated in plasma proteomic signatures of Alzheimer's disease, dementia and cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(37)</ref>.

text.text: Although KLK4 is highly expressed in prostate tissue, whether this contributes to its prominence in the male APOE ε4 carrier signature remains unclear.
MMP12 and TGFBI further highlighted extracellular matrix remodelling and tissue repair, with MMP12 previously associated with future dementia risk (38, 39).
text.formatted: MMP12 and TGFBI further highlighted extracellular matrix remodelling and tissue repair, with MMP12 previously associated with future dementia risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">39)</ref>.

text.text: C1QL2 (40) and KHK (41) pointed towards synaptic organisation and metabolic regulation, respectively.
text.formatted: C1QL2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(40)</ref> and KHK (41) pointed towards synaptic organisation and metabolic regulation, respectively.

text.text: Overall, the male carrier signature emphasised tissue remodelling, cellular communication and metabolic processes.

Although immune-related pathways were represented in both profiles, their underlying components differed, with broader immune and inflammatory signalling featuring in female carriers and innate immune and MAPK-related signalling in male carriers.

Consistent with the importance of sex-specific molecular investigations, a recent study of steroid hormones in Alzheimer's disease identified distinct sex-stratified associations, including elevated cerebrospinal fluid cortisol in females with AD and elevated plasma aldosterone in males with AD (42).
text.formatted: Consistent with the importance of sex-specific molecular investigations, a recent study of steroid hormones in Alzheimer's disease identified distinct sex-stratified associations, including elevated cerebrospinal fluid cortisol in females with AD and elevated plasma aldosterone in males with AD <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(42)</ref>.

text.text: Several proteins captured biological processes shared across female and male APOE ε4 carriers in UKB, with varying degrees of preservation across cohorts.

BCAN and CDCP1 were identified among the top predictors in both female and male APOE ε4 carriers in UKB and remained highly ranked when the UKB-trained models were applied to GNPC, supporting the preservation of these shared molecular signals across cohorts.

In conventional association analyses, BCAN was the only predictor shared between female and male APOE ε4 carriers that showed significant associations with dementia outcomes (all-cause dementia and AD), with these associations observed exclusively among female carriers.

BCAN encodes brevican, a brain-specific extracellular matrix proteoglycan involved in synaptic stabilisation, neuronal plasticity and maintenance of perineuronal nets, and disruption of extracellular matrix organisation has been increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease and cognitive decline (43).
text.formatted: BCAN encodes brevican, a brain-specific extracellular matrix proteoglycan involved in synaptic stabilisation, neuronal plasticity and maintenance of perineuronal nets, and disruption of extracellular matrix organisation has been increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease and cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(43)</ref>.

text.text: CDCP1 has been linked to systemic inflammation, immune activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction (44), processes increasingly recognised as important contributors to dementia pathogenesis.

Although its role in Alzheimer's disease remains incompletely understood, the consistent identification of CDCP1 across APOE ε4 carrier groups suggests that inflammatory mechanisms may contribute to APOE ε4-associated molecular vulnerability.
APOE was also identified among the top predictors in both carrier groups in UKB, although its cross-cohort replication was retained only in female carriers.
APOE plays a central role in lipid transport and cholesterol homeostasis and represents one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease (26).
text.formatted: APOE plays a central role in lipid transport and cholesterol homeostasis and represents one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(26)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that APOE ε4-associated dementia risk may involve altered lipid metabolism alongside disruptions in extracellular matrix organisation and cellular communication.
Despite substantial heterogeneity across strata, GFAP, NEFL and GDF15 were consistently identified among the most important predictors across all four groups in UKB.
This finding is consistent with a previous large-scale UK Biobank proteomic analysis (19), which identified these proteins among the strongest predictors of incident dementia.
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with a previous large-scale UK Biobank proteomic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(19)</ref>, which identified these proteins among the strongest predictors of incident dementia.

text.text: GFAP and NEFL are wellestablished biomarkers of astroglial activation and neuronal injury respectively and have repeatedly demonstrated strong associations with incident dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and cognitive decline (45, 46).
text.formatted: GFAP and NEFL are wellestablished biomarkers of astroglial activation and neuronal injury respectively and have repeatedly demonstrated strong associations with incident dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">46)</ref>.

text.text: GDF15 has emerged as a marker of biological ageing, cellular stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and systemic inflammation, processes increasingly recognised as contributors to neurodegeneration (19).
text.formatted: GDF15 has emerged as a marker of biological ageing, cellular stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and systemic inflammation, processes increasingly recognised as contributors to neurodegeneration <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(19)</ref>.

text.text: The consistent identification of these proteins across strata suggests that neurodegeneration, glial activation, and age-related biological stress represent common pathways underlying dementia risk irrespective of sex and genetic background.
Although NEFL and GDF15 remained common across both APOE ε4 carrier sex strata in GNPC, GFAP showed less consistent preservation.

This may partly reflect differences between the UKB and GNPC cohorts, particularly the contrast between incident dementia prediction in initially dementia-free individuals and prevalent Alzheimer's disease classification in a clinically enriched cohort.
Differences in statistical power may also contribute to this finding.

Plasma GFAP reflects reactive astrogliosis and has been shown to change early in the AD continuum, with elevations observed in cognitively unimpaired individuals with amyloid pathology and years before clinical symptom onset (45) (46) (47).
text.formatted: Plasma GFAP reflects reactive astrogliosis and has been shown to change early in the AD continuum, with elevations observed in cognitively unimpaired individuals with amyloid pathology and years before clinical symptom onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(45)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(46)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(47)</ref>.

text.text: Its relationship with AD pathology may also vary across disease stages.
In contrast, NEFL reflects neuronal injury, while GDF15 captures broader processes related to ageing and cellular stress, which may remain informative across more heterogeneous disease contexts.
NEFL and GFAP were significantly associated with all dementia-related outcomes across all sex and genotype strata.

GDF15 was significantly associated with all three outcomes in female carriers and non-carriers, with VD in male carriers, and with all-cause dementia and AD in male non-carriers (Supplementary Tables 40,42).
text.formatted: GDF15 was significantly associated with all three outcomes in female carriers and non-carriers, with VD in male carriers, and with all-cause dementia and AD in male non-carriers (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">40</ref>,<ref type="table">42</ref>).

text.text: In UKB, SYT1 was among the top predictors in both female and male APOE ε4 carriers, as well as female non-carriers, and conventional association analyses demonstrated significant associations with dementia outcomes in most strata.

SYT1 encodes synaptotagmin-1, a presynaptic vesicle protein involved in calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release and increasingly recognised as a marker of synaptic dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies (48) have reported altered cerebrospinal fluid synaptotagmin-1 concentrations in both preclinical and symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, supporting its role as a marker of early synaptic pathology.
Therefore, SYT1 may reflect a broader synaptic component of dementia risk rather than an APOE ε4-or sex-specific signal.

A major strength of this study is the cross-cohort and cross-platform preservation of molecular feature importance, with SHAP correlations of approximately 0.70 in both sexes despite differences in cohort composition, disease stage, outcome definition (incident all-cause dementia versus prevalent AD) and proteomic platform (Olink versus SomaScan).

Although the highest-ranking predictors across nearly all subgroups were proteins, direct comparison between modalities should be interpreted cautiously given differences in feature numbers and correlations among molecular predictors.
The presence of lipid-related measures among male non-carriers may indicate differential contributions of metabolic pathways across biological risk strata.
Future studies incorporating additional lipidomic and metabolomic platforms may clarify these relationships.
Classifiers excluding age retained broadly comparable discrimination to models including age, although small improvements in AUC were observed with age inclusion in some subgroups.

Given that age is the strongest established risk factor for dementia (2), the preservation of discrimination in models excluding age suggests that the identified omics signatures retain substantial predictive information without chronological age as an explicit predictor.
Current biomarker frameworks are largely applied uniformly across populations despite growing evidence that sex and APOE ε4 status modify Alzheimer's disease biology and progression.

The identification of partially distinct molecular signatures years before incident dementia across sex-APOE ε4 strata suggests that early risk prediction, biomarker interpretation, and potentially future therapeutic targeting may benefit from more biologically stratified and personalised approaches.

The particularly robust molecular signature observed in female APOE ε4 carriers, alongside distinct replicated biological profiles in male carriers, further illustrates how stratification may reveal molecular signals that could be obscured when populations are analysed collectively.
This study has several limitations.
First, the analyses were observational.
Therefore, the identified molecular signatures should be interpreted as predictors and associations rather than evidence of mechanistic causality.
Second, pathway enrichment analyses were exploratory, with no pathways surviving false discovery rate correction; therefore, pathway-level interpretations remain hypothesis-generating.

Nevertheless, the consistency of broader biological themes across SHAP interpretation, enrichment analyses and epidemiological association testing supports the plausibility of the identified sex-specific molecular patterns.
Finally, KNN imputation was performed before cross-validation, potentially introducing information leakage and optimistic bias in performance estimates.

However, a targeted sensitivity analysis in a subset of female APOE ε4 carriers using revised preprocessing showed comparable discrimination and highly correlated predictions, suggesting limited sensitivity to these changes in the evaluated subset.

This study demonstrates that dementia risk is characterised by partially distinct molecular signatures across sex-APOE ε4 strata, with APOE ε4 carriers exhibiting stronger and more reproducible molecular patterns than non-carriers.

The preservation of molecular featureimportance patterns when UKB-trained models were applied to an independent cohort, despite differences in disease stage and proteomic platform, supports their potential biological relevance and transportability.
These findings underscore the importance of stratified approaches for future biomarker discovery, risk prediction and precision medicine strategies in neurodegenerative disease.
The main cohort of the study was the UK Biobank (UKB).
This is a large-scale prospective study including over 500,000 participants in the UK, aged 40-69 years at baseline.
For this study, we were interested in investigating participants with both proteomic and metabolomic data.
UKB Proteomic data was generated using the Olink® Explore 3072 assay (49), and metabolomic data was generated using the Nightingale Health® NMR platform.
text.formatted: UKB Proteomic data was generated using the Olink® Explore 3072 assay <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(49)</ref>, and metabolomic data was generated using the Nightingale Health® NMR platform.

text.text: To identify the overlap between proteomic and metabolomic data, the two datasets were linked at the individual level using the unique UK Biobank participant identifier (eid).
Before quality control, 53,029 participants had proteomics and 488,082 had metabolomics.
Only participants with both proteomic and metabolomic measurements at baseline were retained.
After merging the two datasets, the population of interest was 52,505 participants.
Prevalent dementia cases were removed (n = 55).
Molecules with 25% or more missing data were excluded (n = 4): CST1, GLIPR1, NPM1, and PCOLCE.
In addition, participants with 25% or more missing values across the retained study variables were excluded.
After excluding prevalent dementia cases and applying the missingness criteria, 44,236 participants remained, comprising 1,167 incident dementia cases and 43,069 controls.

Those lost to follow-up were removed as well as participants with no APOE genotype information, resulting in a final sample of 42,605 controls and 1,154 dementia cases with a median follow-up of 15 years (Extended Data Figure 1).
text.formatted: Those lost to follow-up were removed as well as participants with no APOE genotype information, resulting in a final sample of 42,605 controls and 1,154 dementia cases with a median follow-up of 15 years (Extended Data Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: For stratification analyses, the dataset was split by sex and APOE ε4 status, resulting in 23,704 females (APOE ε4 carriers n = 7,007) and 20,055 males (APOE ε4 carriers n = 5,750).
Supplementary Table 2 includes the details of the sample numbers.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref> includes the details of the sample numbers.

text.text: The outcome of interest was all-cause dementia, which included all subtypes of dementia recorded in the UKB.
Dementia cases were identified from linked electronic health records (hospital inpatient records, primary care records, and death certificate registers).
Diagnosis dates were defined as the earliest qualifying dementia diagnosis from these data sources.
The median follow-up duration was 14.6 years (IQR: 13.8-15.3 years).
The key predictors consisted of 3,244 omics (2,917 proteomics and 327 metabolomics).

In addition, age, number of APOE ε4 alleles, ethnicity, years of education and BMI (body mass index) were included based on previous machine learning studies in dementia research (15, 16, 18, 50, 51).

The complete list of proteins used can be found in Supplementary Table 3.

text.text: Metabolomic profiling was performed using high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy by Nightingale Health Ltd.

The platform quantified a broad range of circulating metabolites spanning multiple biological pathways, including lipids and lipoproteins, amino acids, glycolysis-related metabolites, ketone bodies, and other lowmolecular-weight compounds (52).
text.formatted: The platform quantified a broad range of circulating metabolites spanning multiple biological pathways, including lipids and lipoproteins, amino acids, glycolysis-related metabolites, ketone bodies, and other lowmolecular-weight compounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(52)</ref>.

text.text: To minimise technical variation, metabolite measurements were processed using the standard technical correction procedure implemented in the ukbnmr R package.

This approach applies robust linear regression-based correction to the 107 directly measured metabolites to account for known technical confounders, after which derived biomarkers and metabolite ratios are recalculated from the adjusted values.
Additional metabolite ratios proposed within the ukbnmr framework and considered to have potential biological relevance were also included in the present analyses.

A total of 327 metabolite variables were included in the study, comprising 107 directly measured metabolites, 61 composite biomarkers, 81 predefined metabolite ratios, 76 additional metabolite ratios derived using the ukbnmr framework, and two additional Nightingale biomarkers (spectrometer-corrected alanine and glucose-lactate).
The complete list of metabolite measurements is provided in Supplementary Table 4.

text.text: Given the high dimensionality of the dataset and computational constraints, imputation was performed once on the full dataset prior to model development.
Missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbours (k=5), implemented with the KNNImputer class from scikit-learn (53).
text.formatted: Missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbours (k=5), implemented with the KNNImputer class from scikit-learn <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(53)</ref>.

text.text: The choice of k was guided by prior studies applying similar methods to high-dimensional biomedical data (18, 54).

text.text: All classifiers were trained and evaluated on the imputed dataset.
Continuous variables were standardised to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within the nested cross-validation, using the StandardScaler class from scikit-learn.
Standardisation was retained to harmonise feature scales for downstream analyses.
To investigate subgroup-specific molecular risk signatures, the UKB population was stratified by sex and APOE ε4 carrier status.
Sex was defined using UK Biobank Field 31 (female or male), which was obtained from the NHS central registry at recruitment and, in some cases, subsequently updated by participants.
APOE ε4 carriers were defined as individuals with at least one APOE ε4 allele (ε2/ε4, ε3/ε4 or ε4/ε4).
This resulted in four strata: female APOE ε4 carriers, female non-carriers, male APOE ε4 carriers and male non-carriers.
The machine learning pipeline was fitted independently for each stratum.
Baseline characteristics were summarised for the overall cohort and stratified by dementia diagnosis (cases vs. controls).

Continuous variables were summarised as median and interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables (sex, ethnic group, BMI category, and number of APOE ε4 alleles) were summarised as counts and percentages.
Differences between participants with and without dementia were assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and Pearson's chi-squared test for categorical variables.
Two-sided pvalues were reported for descriptive purposes.
Statistical analyses and table generation were performed using Python (SciPy, pandas, and python-docx libraries).
A multivariable logistic regression model was fitted with dementia diagnosis as the binary outcome (0 = no dementia,1 = dementia) using the statsmodels package (v0.14.4) in Python v3.12.9.
The main predictors were APOE ε4 carrier status, sex (binary coded), and their interaction term (APOE ε4 carrier × sex).
Sex was coded as female = 0 and male = 1, while APOE ε4 carrier status was coded as non-carrier = 0 and carrier = 1, with female noncarriers serving as the reference group.

Models were adjusted for age at baseline, years of education, BMI category, and ethnicity (categorised as White, Black and Other/Unknown, with the latter comprising South Asian, Other, Mixed, Chinese and Unknown/NA).
This analysis was intended to assess the interaction between sex and APOE ε4 carrier status on the odds of incident dementia during follow-up, rather than to estimate time to dementia onset.
Variance inflation factors (VIFs) were calculated to assess multicollinearity among predictors.
Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were obtained by exponentiating model coefficients.
Additional contrast-based ORs were computed using linear hypothesis testing (model.t_test) to estimate subgroup-specific effects (e.g., APOE ε4 carriers vs. non-carriers stratified by sex).

XGBoost is an ensemble tree-based machine learning framework built on gradient boosting principles, where sequential decision trees iteratively minimise prediction error by correcting residual errors from preceding trees (55).
text.formatted: XGBoost is an ensemble tree-based machine learning framework built on gradient boosting principles, where sequential decision trees iteratively minimise prediction error by correcting residual errors from preceding trees <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(55)</ref>.

text.text: The method is particularly well suited to highdimensional biomedical data because it can efficiently model nonlinear relationships and complex interactions between variables while remaining robust to complex feature structures (55).
text.formatted: The method is particularly well suited to highdimensional biomedical data because it can efficiently model nonlinear relationships and complex interactions between variables while remaining robust to complex feature structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(55)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, XGBoost is compatible with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) based interpretation, enabling biologically interpretable feature importance analyses.
Given these properties and its strong performance in prior dementia studies (56-59), XGBoost was selected as the classifier in this study.
Independent XGBoost pipelines were developed separately for each subgroup: Female APOE ε4 carriers, Female non-carriers, Male APOE ε4 carriers, and Male non-carriers.

For each subgroup, two independent modelling pipelines were developed using the same preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameter optimisation and evaluation procedures, differing only in whether age was included as a candidate predictor.
This resulted in eight subgroup-specific pipelines.
This comparison was performed to assess the extent to which molecular signatures retained predictive discrimination without chronological age as an explicit model predictor.
The data were split into a training dataset and a testing dataset.
The split, stratified by dementia incidence, was 70/30 i.e., 70% of the data was used for training and 30% to test the classifiers.
The methodology applied to each pipeline is described in detail below.

To reduce dimensionality from over 3,000 features, we applied the Boruta algorithm (BorutaPy implementation) (60) with a Random Forest classifier as the base estimator, separately for each sex-APOE ε4 subgroup.
Categorical variables were converted to categorical type and one-hot encoded; boolean variables were converted to binary format (0/1).
Boruta was applied to the training data only to avoid data leakage.

Training was performed within a repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation framework (with 3 repeats), using n_estimators='auto' to allow BorutaPy to determine the number of trees automatically, perc=100 to retain only features with importance greater than the most important shadow feature (minimising false positives), and a maximum of 50 iterations to balance stability with computational efficiency.
Balanced class weights were used to address class imbalance.
A feature was deemed stable if selected in ≥40% of all cross-validation runs.
Stable features for each subgroup were retained for subsequent machine learning model development, with the selected feature set held fixed throughout nested cross-validation.

For each sex-APOE ε4 subgroup, we trained gradient-boosted tree models using XGBoost within a repeated nested cross-validation framework (outer 5-fold CV; inner 3-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning; repeated 5 times).

Models were fit on the Boruta-selected feature set (stability ≥ 0.40), retrieved from the original dataset and preprocessed within the final modelling pipeline (continuous variables standardised using a StandardScaler fitted on the corresponding model-fitting data, categorical variables one-hot encoded, and boolean variables converted to binary).
Class imbalance was addressed using scale_pos_weight, computed as the ratio of negative to positive cases in the training dataset.
All models used GPU acceleration with histogram-based tree growth (tree_method='hist', device='cuda').
Hyperparameters were optimised by randomised search (10 iterations, ROC-AUC scoring) over predefined ranges (Supplementary Table 5).
text.formatted: Hyperparameters were optimised by randomised search (10 iterations, ROC-AUC scoring) over predefined ranges (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: For each subgroup, the best hyperparameters selected by the inner 3-fold cross-validation within each outer training fold were aggregated across the 25 outer-fold iterations (5 folds × 5 repetitions) to obtain a single configuration for final model fitting, reducing dependence on any individual training partition.
Numerical hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, subsample) were aggregated by taking the mean, while categorical hyperparameters (e.g., booster type) were aggregated using the mode.
During nested cross-validation, decision thresholds were selected separately using predictions from each outer validation fold to achieve specificity ≥ 0.85 while maximising recall.
The mean threshold across outer folds was used to generate the aggregated cross-validation confusion matrix.
The final XGBoost model was retrained on the training set using the aggregated hyperparameters derived from nested cross-validation.

For probability calibration, the training data were further split into sub-training (80%) and calibration (20%) subsets, stratified by dementia status; the XGBoost classifier was refitted on the sub-training subset and subsequently calibrated using sigmoid regression (CalibratedClassifierCV, method = "sigmoid", cv = "prefit"), fitted on the calibration subset.

For the final calibrated model, the decision threshold was selected on the calibration subset using the same criterion (specificity ≥ 0.85 while maximising recall) and subsequently applied to the held-out test set.
Model performance was evaluated on the independent held-out test set using calibrated probabilities.
Performance metrics included discrimination (ROC-AUC), calibration (Brier score), accuracy, specificity, recall, precision, and F1 score.
Threshold-dependent metrics and confusion matrices were calculated using the previously selected calibration-derived threshold.
To assess potential data leakage arising from KNN imputation performed before the trainingtest split, a targeted sensitivity analysis was conducted in a subset of 2,000 female APOE ε4 carriers.
The analysis used 68 previously selected features from models excluding age as a predictor and a fixed XGBoost configuration.
Both preprocessing approaches were evaluated using the same stratified 70/30 training-test split.

The original approach, in which KNN imputation was fitted to the full dataset before splitting, was compared with a revised approach in which imputation was fitted exclusively on the training data and subsequently applied to the test data.
Model discrimination was evaluated using AUC, and agreement between predicted probabilities was assessed using Pearson's correlation coefficient.
Two complementary bootstrap procedures were applied.

First, for each subgroup's final model, uncertainty in performance metrics (ROC-AUC, recall, precision, F1 score, specificity, and accuracy) was quantified by stratified bootstrap resampling of the held-out test set with replacement (1,000 replicates).
Dementia cases and controls were resampled separately, retaining the original sample size of each group in every replicate.
Point estimates were paired with 95% percentile confidence intervals derived from the bootstrap distributions.

Second, to directly compare discrimination between the with-age and no-age pipelines, paired nonparametric bootstrap resampling was performed on the same held-out test set (1,000 stratified replicates).
Within each replicate, cases and controls were resampled with replacement, and the same bootstrap indices were applied to both models before recomputing ROC-AUC.
The difference in AUC (ΔAUC; AUCwith-age -AUCno-age) was recorded across replicates.
We report the observed ΔAUC and its 95% percentile bootstrap confidence interval, calculated from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.

Bootstrap resampling was selected because it does not rely on parametric distributional assumptions and enables robust estimation of uncertainty for performance metrics, as well as paired comparison of models evaluated on the same individuals.
Feature importance and interpretation were computed using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) (61), implemented with shap.Explainer applied to the trained XGBoost estimator.
SHAP values were calculated on the transformed held-out test set, using the correspondingly transformed training set as the background dataset.
Global feature importance was summarised as the mean absolute SHAP value for each feature, and features were ranked accordingly.
SHAP summary and bar plots were generated to visualise the direction, magnitude, and relative importance of feature contributions.
For reproducibility, we report the SHAP details used in Supplementary Table 6.

text.text: Pathway enrichment analyses were conducted as an exploratory approach to identify biological themes associated with sex-specific differences in UKB SHAP-derived protein importance rankings.
Enrichment was performed using a pre-ranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) approach implemented in the clusterProfiler and ReactomePA packages in R (v4.4.0).

To investigate biological processes associated with sex differences in model-derived protein importance, separate female-versus-male contrasts were generated for APOE ε4 carriers and APOE ε4 non-carriers.
For each comparison, proteins were ranked using mean absolute SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values obtained from the subgroup-specific UKB XGBoost models.
Protein importance values from the female and male models were merged using the union of proteins retained in either model.
Proteins absent from a subgroup-specific model were assigned a SHAP importance of zero, reflecting their absence from that fitted model.

This approach was intended to compare the complete model-derived protein signatures, capturing differences in both feature selection and relative SHAP importance between sexes, rather than estimating intrinsic sex-specific biological effects.
To account for differences in the distributions of SHAP importance between independently trained models, mean absolute SHAP values were standardised within each sex using z-score transformation.
This allowed the subsequent contrast to capture differences in relative feature importance between the sex-specific predictive signatures, rather than differences in absolute SHAP magnitudes.

A contrast score was then calculated for each protein as the difference between the standardised female and male SHAP values (female minus male), such that positive values indicated greater relative importance in females and negative values indicated greater relative importance in males.
Protein symbols were mapped to Entrez Gene identifiers using the org.Hs.eg.db annotation database.
Where multiple proteins mapped to the same Entrez identifier, the protein with the largest absolute contrast score was retained.
Proteins were then ranked according to their contrast scores to generate a pre-ranked gene list for enrichment analysis.

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis was performed using the gseGO() function against Gene Ontology Biological Process (GO:BP) terms and the gsePathway() function against the Reactome pathway database, using nPermSimple = 10,000.
Multiple testing correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
Only gene sets containing between 5 and 500 genes were considered.

Enrichment results were summarised using normalised enrichment scores (NES), where positive NES values indicate pathways enriched among proteins with greater relative importance in females and negative NES values indicate pathways enriched among proteins with greater relative importance in males.
Results were visualised using custom dot plots displaying pathway enrichment direction, gene set size, and false discovery rate-adjusted significance.

To evaluate cross-platform transportability of the UKB proteomic signal, external validation was performed using the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) v1 harmonized dataset (21), accessed through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) AD Workbench (62).
text.formatted: To evaluate cross-platform transportability of the UKB proteomic signal, external validation was performed using the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) v1 harmonized dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(21)</ref>, accessed through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) AD Workbench <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(62)</ref>.

text.text: GNPC is a harmonised multi-cohort proteomics resource enriched for neurodegenerative disorders, including AD, Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
External validation analyses were restricted to APOE ε4 carrier subgroups, as these models showed the strongest performance in UKB.
In addition, the models chosen for validation were the models not including age as a predictor given the robust performance in UKB.
Only GNPC baseline visits were included in the present analysis.

This external validation framework represents a stringent test of cross-cohort transportability due to substantial differences between datasets, including disease stage (incident dementia in UKB versus prevalent dementia in GNPC), outcome definition (all-cause dementia in UKB versus clinically diagnosed AD in GNPC), proteomic platform (Olink in UKB versus SomaScan in GNPC), and cohort age structure.

Proteomic measurements in GNPC were generated using SomaScan SOMAmer technology (versions 3, 4, and 4.1), comprising approximately 7,000 aptamers per sample, whereas UKB proteomics were measured using the Olink platform.
Preprocessing and harmonisation of the GNPC v1 dataset were performed as previously described by the consortium (21).
text.formatted: Preprocessing and harmonisation of the GNPC v1 dataset were performed as previously described by the consortium <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(21)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, we standardised GNPC protein abundance values using z-score normalisation, centring each protein to mean zero and scaling to unit variance.
Cohort-specific standardisation was applied to harmonise feature scales while avoiding transfer of distributional parameters across proteomic platforms.
Neither carrier-specific model retained metabolomic predictors following feature selection; therefore, no metabolite imputation was required for external validation in GNPC.
UKB Olink protein predictors were mapped to GNPC SomaScan proteins by protein symbol.
Where multiple SomaScan aptamers corresponded to a single protein, aptamer values were collapsed using the median abundance across aptamers.

For UKB model predictors not measured in GNPC, a constant value corresponding to the UKB training-set mean was initially assigned to all GNPC participants, thereby preserving the original model input structure.
Following GNPC-specific z-score standardisation, these constant-valued predictors became undefined (NaN) due to zero variance and were handled by XGBoost's native missing-value mechanism.
This pragmatic approach enabled application of the original UKB models without refitting.
Feature ordering was matched exactly to the original UKB training matrices separately for female and male APOE ε4 carrier models before prediction.
The primary outcome in GNPC was AD diagnosis.
Cases were defined as individuals with AD diagnosis (AD = 1).
Controls were defined as individuals without AD diagnosis (AD = 0) and with a Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score <0.5.
text.formatted: Controls were defined as individuals without AD diagnosis (AD = 0) and with a Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score <0.5.

text.text: Individuals not meeting either definition were excluded from analysis.
Final UKB-trained XGBoost classifiers were exported in UBJSON format and applied directly to GNPC without retraining.

The female APOE ε4 carrier model retained 1,000 boosting rounds and 68 input features, while the male APOE ε4 carrier model retained 1000 boosting rounds and 71 input features, confirming preservation of the original UKB-trained architectures.
Predicted probabilities were generated after harmonising GNPC predictors to the corresponding UKB feature order.
Classification thresholds previously optimised and calibrated in UKB were transferred unchanged to GNPC for external evaluation.
Performance metrics included ROC-AUC, recall, specificity, precision, F1 score, and accuracy.
To assess biological concordance across cohorts, SHAP values were computed for the externally validated GNPC predictions using the UKB-trained XGBoost models.
Global feature importance was summarised using mean absolute SHAP values.
Concordance between UKB and GNPC feature importance rankings was assessed using Spearman correlation across shared proteins.
Overlap among the top-ranked proteins between cohorts was additionally quantified, and concordance plots were generated to visualise preservation of feature importance structure across datasets.

Exploratory, post-hoc association analyses were conducted to further characterise the relationships between proteins identified as replicated predictors across UKB and GNPC and multiple dementia-related outcomes within UKB APOE ε4 carrier populations, stratified by sex.

As protein selection was partly informed by predictive importance within the same cohort, these analyses were intended to provide complementary epidemiological characterisation rather than independent confirmatory evidence.
Specifically, proteins consistently ranked among the top 20 predictors in both UKB and GNPC for each sex-specific APOE ε4 carrier group were selected for these association analyses.

GFAP was additionally included in both sex-specific analyses because it was consistently identified across all UKB sex and APOE ε4 strata and has been widely implicated in early neurodegeneration (45, 46).
text.formatted: GFAP was additionally included in both sex-specific analyses because it was consistently identified across all UKB sex and APOE ε4 strata and has been widely implicated in early neurodegeneration <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">46)</ref>.

text.text: APOE and SYT1 were also included in the male carrier analysis because they ranked among the top predictors in the corresponding UKB model and replicated in female carriers.

Analyses were performed separately in female and male APOE ε4 carriers using multivariable logistic regression implemented in Python (v3.12.9) with pandas (v2.2.3), numpy (v2.1.3), and statsmodels (v0.14).
For each sex-specific analysis, only individuals carrying one or two APOE ε4 alleles were included.
Three binary outcomes were evaluated independently: allcause dementia, Alzheimer's disease (AD), and vascular dementia (VD).
These outcomes were not mutually exclusive, and participants with multiple dementia diagnoses could contribute as cases to more than one analysis.
To ensure outcome specificity, a shared "healthy control" group was defined as individuals free from all three diagnoses simultaneously (Dementia = 0, AD = 0, and VD = 0).
For each outcome, cases were compared against this common control population, to avoid contamination of controls with alternative dementia diagnoses.
Proteomic predictors were analysed individually, with a separate multivariable logistic regression model fitted for each protein-outcome combination.
Protein abundance values were standardised to z-scores prior to analysis, while continuous covariates (age at baseline and years of education) were similarly z-score normalised.
APOE ε4 allele count (1 or 2 copies) was modelled as a continuous gene-dose covariate, and categorical covariates (ethnic_group and BMI_levels) were encoded using categorical dummy variables.
Models were adjusted for age at baseline, APOE ε4 allele count (included as a numeric gene-dose covariate), years of education, ethnicity, and BMI category.
Robust HC3 standard errors were used to reduce sensitivity to heteroscedasticity.
Associations were summarised as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Multiple testing correction was performed separately within each sex-specific analysis and dementia outcome, across the proteins tested, using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.
Statistical significance was defined as FDR q < 0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was defined as FDR q < 0.05.

text.text: Results were visualised using heatmaps of log₂(OR), volcano plots, and forest plots of FDR-significant associations.

To further investigate the association of shared predictors across all strata with multiple dementia outcomes, sex-stratified multivariable logistic regression analyses were additionally conducted in the APOE ε4 non-carrier populations following the same analytical framework described in the previous Section.
GFAP, GDF15 and NEFL were selected because they were consistently identified among the top predictors across all UKB sex and APOE ε4 strata.
SYT1 protein was additionally included because it was identified among the top predictors in all UKB strata except male non-carriers.

These analyses aimed to determine whether the shared predictors identified through the prediction models were also associated with multiple dementia outcomes in conventional association analyses for the non-carrier population.
